query: For high-entropy-alloy bond coats used in thermal barrier coating systems for high-temperature applications, what single intervention could improve coating durability and reliability? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted improvement relative to an untreated baseline, the conditions under which it should remain effective, prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small fraction of zirconium to the high‐entropy alloy bond coat will form a graded interfacial layer that enhances metallurgical bonding and oxidation resistance, thereby reducing oxide scale spallation under high-temperature cyclic conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: Standard high‐entropy alloy bond coat (e.g., without reactive element modification) used in thermal barrier coating systems.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled low concentration of zirconium (via alloying/doping during deposition) into the HEA bond coat formulation.
generation.conditions: High-temperature (up to ~900°C) oxidizing and corrosive environments with thermal cycling similar to those in gas turbines or steam pipelines.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a graded, Zr-enriched interfacial layer (e.g., a gradient HfZr or Zr-rich phase) at the bond coat–substrate interface.
generation.mechanism: The added zirconium diffuses during processing and subsequent high-temperature exposure to form a graded interfacial layer. This graded layer improves adhesion by reducing thermal expansion mismatch and promoting stronger metallurgical bonding, while also acting as a barrier to oxygen diffusion, thereby mitigating oxide scale spallation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated bond coat, the Zr-doped bond coat is expected to show a lower rate of oxide spallation, improved adhesion strength, and enhanced overall durability under repeated high-temperature exposure.
generation.baseline: HEA bond coats without zirconium modification, which are more prone to interfacial delamination and oxide spallation under high-temperature cyclic conditions.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected for optimal Zr levels in the low to moderate range; excessive Zr or operation beyond ~900°C may lead to undesirable phase formation or brittleness.
generation.uncertainty: Exact optimal Zr content and quantitative improvement in adhesion and spallation resistance remain to be determined; long-term cyclic performance under varying environmental conditions also requires further study.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of bond coat samples on an identical substrate: one set using the conventional HEA composition and a second set with a controlled addition of zirconium. Subject both sets to high-temperature cyclic oxidation tests (e.g., 900°C in a corrosive salt environment) for a predetermined number of cycles. Assess coating adhesion, extent of oxide spallation, and interfacial microstructure using microscopy and quantitative adhesion (pull-off) tests.
measurements: Percentage of the coating area exhibiting spallation
Adhesion strength measured by pull-off tests
Microstructural examination of the bond coat–substrate interface (to determine the presence and quality of the graded Zr-rich layer)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the zirconium-doped bond coats do not show a statistically significant (e.g., >10% reduction in spallation area and ≥15% improvement in adhesion strength) improvement over the conventional HEA coats, or if no graded Zr-enriched interfacial layer is observed, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The distribution of carbon element, indicate that hafnium on the coating surface and carbon paper formed hafnium coating during the hot-press sintering process, but the thickness of HfC coating is less than 10 μm due to the limited diffusive distance of carbon element. The carbon at the interface between the substrate and the coating mainly originates from the mixture of metal hafnium prepared by electro-deoxygenation and HfC powder in the coating, and the diffusive distance is similar to the thickness of the surface HfC. The cathode carbon deposition of the electrode-oxidation process is caused by the side reaction of soluble CO3− and calcium ions, which can be described by the following reactions: The deposited carbon forms HfC with the metal Hf prepared by cathode deoxidation and the HfC coating is formed in the process of hot-pressing sintering to prepare the coating. The migration of zirconium elements at the interface between the coating and the substrate helps to improve the bondability between the coating and the substrate, thus effectively improving the protection of the coating against the substrate.
